Record date: 2130-01-31
South Elizabeth Seychelles Hospital INTERNAL MEDICINE DEPARTMENT Location: 4923 Olivia Parkway Suite 217, Lake Jennabury
PATIENT: Lysander Fairfax Phone: 28451903 email:bradleymorgan@example.org DATE OF BIRTH: 1947-05-12 AGE: 80 years
FOLLOW-UP DATE: 01/31/30 FOLLOWED BY: Dr. Emily Carter
CHIEF COMPLAINT
Persistent shortness of breath and productive cough with changes in sputum color.
HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Mr. Lysander Fairfax returns for a follow-up visit two days after his last consultation. He reports that while his cough remains productive, the sputum has now changed to a greenish hue, raising concerns for possible secondary bacterial infection. He continues to experience significant dyspnea, particularly with exertion, and describes a marked increase in fatigue, which he attributes to his ongoing respiratory distress.
Mr. Fairfax notes that his night sweats have persisted, and he has experienced intermittent chills. He denies any new fevers but mentions that he feels generally unwell. His epigastric discomfort remains stable, and he reports that his heartburn symptoms have improved since the adjustment of his Omeprazole.
REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
General - + profound fatigue, + night sweats, - weight loss, - chills. Pulmonary - + productive cough with green sputum, + significant dyspnea, + wheezing, - hemoptysis. Cardiac - no chest pain, - orthopnea, - paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea. Gastrointestinal - + mild epigastric discomfort, + improved heartburn, - nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea. Musculoskeletal - no joint pain. Neurological - no dizziness or headaches.
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital Signs: - Blood Pressure: 130/82 mmHg - Heart Rate: 90 bpm - Respiratory Rate: 30 breaths/min - Oxygen Saturation: 82% on supplemental oxygen (10 L via nasal cannula).
General: The patient appears fatigued and is in moderate respiratory distress, utilizing accessory muscles for breathing.
HEENT: No nasal flaring; oropharynx clear, no signs of dehydration.
Lungs: Persistent wheezing on auscultation; diminished breath sounds bilaterally; prolonged expiration with rhonchi; audible crackles noted throughout lung fields, particularly in the lower lobes.
Cardiac: Regular rate and rhythm; no murmurs or gallops; peripheral pulses intact.
Abdomen: Soft, non-tender; mild epigastric discomfort noted; no hepatosplenomegaly.
ASSESSMENT
1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) exacerbation with possible secondary bacterial infection, as indicated by the change in sputum color and persistent respiratory symptoms. 2. Intravenous antibiotic therapy with Ceftriaxone has not yielded the desired improvement in respiratory status; sputum culture results are pending. 3. Fatigue and dyspnea remain significant, likely exacerbated by the respiratory infection; gastrointestinal symptoms continue to improve.
PLAN
1. Review sputum culture and sensitivity results as soon as available; consider transitioning to a broader spectrum antibiotic, such as Piperacillin-tazobactam, if results indicate resistant organisms or if clinical deterioration occurs. 2. Continue intravenous Ceftriaxone 1 g every 24 hours for now; maintain oral Prednisone at 60 mg daily, with plans for gradual tapering based on clinical response; continue Omeprazole at 40 mg daily for gastric protection. 3. Increase supplemental oxygen to 12 L via nasal cannula; closely monitor respiratory status and prepare for potential escalation to BiPAP therapy if hypoxemia persists. 4. Schedule a repeat chest X-ray to assess for any complications, such as pleural effusion or worsening pneumonia. 5. Continue nebulized bronchodilator therapy (Albuterol) every four hours as needed; initiate Ipratropium bromide for enhanced bronchodilation. 6. Arrange for a follow-up visit within 48 hours to reassess respiratory function, medication response, and overall clinical condition; consider early involvement of a pulmonologist for specialized management.
DISPOSITION
Mr. Fairfax remains under close observation in the internal medicine unit. The treatment team will continue to adapt the management plan based on his clinical trajectory, with particular emphasis on respiratory function and the evolving gastrointestinal symptoms. Patient education will be reinforced regarding the importance of adherence to the antibiotic regimen and the need to report any new or worsening symptoms, including increased sputum production or changes in color.
